morning-fajr.text: Win the morning with Fajr on time — the rest of the day follows a calmer rhythm.

witr-closure.text: Close your night with witr when you can — a gentle seal on the day's worship.

return-tomorrow.text: If today was hard, begin again after maghrib. Mercy is wider than one difficult day.

tasbeeh-count.text: A short tasbeeh session counts. Zikr is not only for long sittings — start with ten.

tahajjud.summary: The night prayer offered in the last third of the night, before Fajr.
tahajjud.why: Allah descends to the lowest heaven in the last third of the night and asks who will call upon Him. The Prophet ﷺ regularly prayed at night even when optional for him.
tahajjud.benefits: Draws one closer to Allah, softens the heart, and was the habit of the righteous before him. A time when dua is especially answered.

fajr.summary: The dawn prayer — the first of the five daily obligatory prayers.
fajr.why: Allah commanded establishing prayer at the edges of the day; Fajr marks the start of the Muslim day and was never abandoned by the Prophet ﷺ in congregation or alone.
fajr.benefits: Whoever prays Fajr is under Allah's protection. It is witnessed by the angels of the night and day and brings light for the rest of the day.

sunrise.summary: The moment the sun rises above the horizon — a time marker, not a prayer itself.
sunrise.why: Prayer is forbidden while the sun is rising (and at zenith and setting) so the ummah does not resemble sun-worshippers. Knowing sunrise helps time Ishraq and avoid invalid prayer times.
sunrise.benefits: Observing Allah's signs in the sky increases awe (taqwa) and helps structure the morning Sunnah prayers correctly.

ishraq.summary: A two-rakah Sunnah prayer after the sun has fully risen (about 15–20 minutes after sunrise).
ishraq.why: The Prophet ﷺ said whoever prays Fajr in congregation then sits remembering Allah until sunrise, then prays two rakahs, receives the reward of a complete Hajj and 'Umrah.
ishraq.benefits: Immense reward with minimal effort when combined with Fajr in congregation. A peaceful start to the day in Zikr and optional prayer.

duha.summary: The forenoon prayer — typically two to eight rakahs between sunrise and Dhuhr.
duha.why: Charity is due on every joint of the body each day; even a few rakahs of Duha fulfills that charity for the limbs through worship.
duha.benefits: Forgives sins, brings sustenance (rizq), and revives a neglected Sunnah. Flexible timing makes it accessible when the day allows.

dhuhr.summary: The midday prayer — the second obligatory prayer, when the sun passes its zenith.
dhuhr.why: The five daily prayers were made obligatory on the Night Journey; Dhuhr breaks the day's busyness with remembrance of Allah.
dhuhr.benefits: The Prophet ﷺ said the first deed judged on the Day of Resurrection is prayer. Guarding Dhuhr protects the rest of one's deeds.

asr.summary: The afternoon prayer — the middle prayer emphasized in the Qur'an.
asr.why: Allah specifically warns about guarding the middle prayer (Salat al-Wusta). It falls when many are busy or tired, so preserving it is a sign of sincerity.
asr.benefits: Whoever misses Asr, it is as if he lost his family and wealth — highlighting its weight. Keeping it strengthens discipline through the day.

maghrib.summary: The sunset prayer — prayed immediately after the sun has set.
maghrib.why: The time opens right at sunset; delaying without reason risks missing the preferred window. The Prophet ﷺ warned against neglecting prayer until the sun has set.
maghrib.benefits: Marks gratitude at the day's end and was among the first prayers the Prophet ﷺ emphasized to his companions.

isha.summary: The night prayer — the last of the five obligatory prayers, after twilight fades.
isha.why: Completes the cycle of daily worship. The Prophet ﷺ said if someone prayed Isha in congregation, it is as if he prayed half the night.
isha.benefits: Brings tranquility before sleep and completes the day's fard prayers. Often followed by Witr, which is Sunnah mu'akkadah.

witr.summary: An odd-numbered prayer (usually one or three rakahs) after Isha before Fajr — Sunnah mu'akkadah, not one of the five fard prayers.
witr.why: The Prophet ﷺ said Allah is Witr (One) and loves Witr, so maintain the Witr prayer. He never abandoned it, even when traveling.
witr.benefits: A distinctive mark of the believer's night routine. Closing the day with odd-numbered prayer aligns with Allah's names and the Prophet's consistent practice.

tahiyyatul_masjid.summary: Two rakahs greeting the masjid when entering, before sitting.
tahiyyatul_masjid.why: When one of you enters the masjid, let him pray two rakahs before sitting — a direct instruction of the Prophet ﷺ.
tahiyyatul_masjid.benefits: Honors the house of Allah, prepares the heart for congregation or private worship, and replaces idle sitting with immediate good.

hajat_istikhara.summary: Optional prayers for personal needs (Salat al-Hajah) and seeking Allah's guidance (Salat al-Istikhara).
hajat_istikhara.why: Istikhara is to ask Allah to choose good for you when facing a decision. Hajah is to present one's need to Allah through prayer before or alongside dua.
hajat_istikhara.benefits: Builds reliance on Allah (tawakkul) instead of anxiety alone. Istikhara brings clarity; Hajah pairs worship with sincere request — and Allah answers those who call upon Him.

witrNote.title: Is Witr Qaza required?
witrNote.intro: According to the majority of scholars, making up a missed Witr is allowed, but whether it is required depends on your madhhab (school of thought).
witrNote.hanafiBody: Witr is wajib (obligatory). If you miss it, you must make it up (Qaza). Pray it as soon as you remember — even if days or weeks have passed. This is the view followed by most Muslims in South Asia, Central Asia, and Turkey.
witrNote.othersBody: Witr is a strongly emphasized Sunnah (Sunnah mu'akkadah), not obligatory. Making it up is recommended (mustahabb) but not required. The Prophet ﷺ would make up night prayers missed due to sleep or illness.
witrNote.evidenceBody: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever sleeps and misses Witr or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers." (Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah — scholars differ on its grading.) In Sahih Muslim, when he missed night prayer due to illness or sleep, he made it up during the day with an even number of rakahs.
witrNote.footer: This app counts missed Witr toward Qaza for all users. Treat it as required if you follow the Hanafi view; otherwise track it as a recommended make-up. Consult a scholar for your situation.

travel.title: Traveling & Salah
travel.subtitle: Qasr, Jam', and what the Qur'an and Sunnah teach about Salah on a journey
travel.takeaway: Allah legislated shortening (Qasr) and combining (Jam') out of mercy for the traveler — not to abandon prayer, but to ease its performance on the road.
travel.obligationsTitle: What you are still responsible for
travel.rakatsNote: Only the fard is shown. Sunnah rawatib and Witr are discussed below — they remain recommended, though many travelers lighten them for hardship.

quran.excerpt: When you travel through the land, there is no blame on you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are ever a clear enemy to you.

hadith.excerpt: Anas said: We travelled with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The mu'adhin called for prayer and he said: 'Pray two rakahs' — and he did the same for the other prayers except Maghrib (three) and Fajr (two).
Ibn Abbas said: The Prophet ﷺ combined Dhuhr and Asr, and Maghrib and Isha in Madinah without fear or rain. When asked why, he said: 'He wanted not to burden his Ummah.'

Ya'la ibn Umayyah said: I said to Umar ibn al-Khattab: 'There is no sin if one shortens the prayer while travelling.' Umar replied: 'I wondered the same, so I asked the Prophet ﷺ and he said: It is charity from Allah — accept His charity.'
The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Allah loves that His concessions be taken, just as He hates to be disobeyed.'

obligations: The five daily prayers remain obligatory — shortened (Qasr) when you qualify as a traveler.
Fajr (two rakahs) and Maghrib (three rakahs) are never shortened.
You may combine Dhuhr with Asr, and Maghrib with Isha, when the conditions of travel apply.
Each shortened prayer is prayed like the first two rakahs of the full prayer — recite Al-Fatiha and a surah, bow, prostrate, then sit for tashahhud and salam.
When you return home or intend to settle, resume praying each prayer in full at its proper time.
Missed prayers while traveling must still be made up (Qaza) — travel does not waive what was omitted.

qasr.title: Qasr — shortening
qasr.body: The four-rakah fard prayers — Dhuhr, Asr, and Isha — are prayed as two rakahs on a qualifying journey. Pray them exactly as the first two rakahs at home: standing recitation, one ruku, two sujud, tashahhud, and salam. Fajr stays two rakahs and Maghrib stays three; neither is shortened. Qasr applies to the fard only.

jam.title: Jam' — combining
jam.body: A traveler may combine Dhuhr with Asr into one sitting, and Maghrib with Isha into one sitting — praying both fard prayers back-to-back with one Adhan and iqamah. Fajr cannot be combined with any other prayer. Combining is a separate concession from shortening: you may shorten without combining, combine without shortening (in some situations), or do both together.

jamTypes.title: Jam' al-Taqdim & al-Ta'khir
jamTypes.body: Jam' al-Taqdim (early combining): pray both prayers together at the earlier prayer's time — e.g. Dhuhr and Asr at Dhuhr time. Jam' al-Ta'khir (delayed combining): pray both at the later prayer's time — e.g. Dhuhr and Asr at Asr time. At Arafah the Prophet ﷺ brought Asr forward to Dhuhr time, and at Muzdalifah he delayed Maghrib to Isha time — one example of each form (Sahih Muslim 1218).

when.title: When concessions begin & end
when.body: Concessions begin once you leave your town or city on a journey — not for daily commutes within your locality. They end when you return home, or when you intend to stay at your destination for the period scholars define as 'settling' (the number of days differs between schools). If you are unsure whether you still count as a traveler, ask a scholar before assuming the concessions.

distance.title: Travel distance
distance.body: Most scholars require a minimum travel distance before Qasr and Jam' apply — commonly cited as roughly 80 km (48 miles), or about two days' journey on foot. Some schools measure from the last buildings of one's city; others use a shorter threshold. The app does not calculate this for you — know your school's criterion and apply it with a scholar's guidance.

sunnah.title: Sunnah Salah while traveling
sunnah.body: The emphasized Sunnah prayers (rawatib) before and after fard remain virtuous but are not required. Many scholars permit leaving them while traveling due to hardship, especially when combining prayers. The greeting of the masjid (tahiyyatul masjid) and other voluntary prayers remain permissible whenever you have time and energy.

witr.title: Witr on a journey
witr.body: Witr is Sunnah mu'akkadah (strongly emphasized) and should not be abandoned while traveling. Pray it after Isha — even if you combined Maghrib and Isha — as one, three, or more odd rakahs according to what you can manage. If you fear sleeping before Isha while traveling, the Prophet ﷺ permitted praying Witr earlier after the combined Maghrib-Isha.

travel.disclaimer: This is educational content, not a personal fatwa. Distance thresholds, stay duration, combining rules, and whether Jam' is limited to need vary between the four schools — consult a qualified scholar for your journey.

hayd.title: Hayd & worship
hayd.subtitle: What the texts teach about menstruation and daily acts of worship
hayd.obligationsTitle: What you are still responsible for

hadith.excerpt: Aisha said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'When your menses ends, perform ghusl and then pray.'
The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Is it not the case that when one of you menstruates, she neither prays nor fasts?'

obligations: Do not offer Salah while in hayd — this is Allah's concession, not neglect of worship.
Do not fast during hayd; any missed Ramadan fasts must be made up afterward.
You may still make Zikr, dua, listen to Qur'an, give charity, and other good deeds.
When hayd ends, perform ghusl and resume Salah and fasting.

duration.title: Duration of hayd
duration.body:
Hayd is the regular monthly bleeding most women experience at a familiar time each cycle. Scholars discuss a minimum duration (some say one day and night, others require more) and a maximum duration — commonly cited figures range from about 10 to 15 days depending on the school of thought.

Practically, note your usual pattern (‘ada): how many days hayd typically lasts and when it usually begins. If bleeding continues beyond the maximum hayd duration in your school, the extra days may be treated as istihada — the rules of prayer and fasting change once hayd ends, even if bleeding continues.

istihada.title: Istihada — irregular bleeding
istihada.body:
Istihada is bleeding outside the normal hayd period — between cycles, after puberty before the first regular period, or when bleeding continues past the maximum hayd duration.

Unlike hayd, istihada does not lift the obligation to pray and fast. A woman with istihada generally performs wudu for each prayer while bleeding is active; the bleeding itself does not invalidate wudu according to many scholars.

Distinguishing hayd from istihada can be difficult. Women with a known cycle often rely on their habit, the time of the month, and the characteristics of the blood. If you are unsure whether bleeding is hayd or istihada, pause obligatory tracking only when you are confident it is hayd, and consult a qualified scholar for your specific case.

nifas.title: Nifas — postpartum bleeding
nifas.body:
Nifas is bleeding after childbirth. The same broad rules as hayd apply: Salah and fasting are not performed during nifas, and missed Ramadan fasts are made up afterward — not the prayers.

Maximum duration differs by school; 40 days is commonly mentioned. When nifas ends, perform ghusl and resume all worship. Nifas and hayd are separate categories — a woman may experience both at different times in her life.

purity.title: When bleeding ends — ghusl & resumption
purity.body:
When hayd or nifas ends, perform a full ghusl before resuming Salah. Resume fasting only after hayd ends; any Ramadan fasts missed during hayd must be made up on other days.

Salah missed during hayd is not made up — Allah lifted that obligation. This is different from illness or travel, where missed prayers may need Qaza. After ghusl, resume your normal worship and obligatory tracking in the app.

hayd.disclaimer: This is educational guidance, not a personal ruling. The details above vary between schools — consult a qualified female scholar if your situation is unclear.

sick.title: Illness & Salah
sick.subtitle: Concessions for sickness and what remains upon you
sick.obligationsTitle: What you are still responsible for

hadith.excerpt: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on your side.'
The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Allah has removed from my Ummah mistakes, forgetfulness, and what they are forced to do.'
Imran ibn Husayn had a painful condition and prayed sitting. The Prophet ﷺ asked him: 'Can you stand?' He said no, so the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Then pray sitting; if you cannot, then lying on your side.'

obligations: If you are able, pray in whatever position you can — standing, sitting, or lying down.
Reduce or omit bowing and prostration only when you genuinely cannot perform them.

As long as you are conscious, Salah is not dropped — pray however you can, even by gesture. Salah missed through illness is made up (Qaza) when you recover; if you were unconscious, the schools differ on whether it must be made up.
Missed Ramadan fasts due to illness should be made up when you are able.
You may still make Zikr, dua, read Qur'an, and give charity.

positions.title: Praying while ill — positions
positions.body:
The default is to pray standing with full ruku and sujud. If standing causes severe pain, weakness, or harm, pray sitting — many scholars permit sitting even without standing first when illness makes standing genuinely difficult.

If you cannot sit upright, pray lying on your side or back, gesturing for ruku and sujud with your head. Use every position concession before skipping a prayer entirely.

If you cannot use water for wudu because of illness or risk of harm, perform tayammum when its conditions are met.

rukuSujud.title: Ruku & sujud with limited movement
rukuSujud.body:
When you cannot perform full bowing, incline your head for ruku — a deeper incline for sujud. This is the concession used when praying sitting or lying down.

If you cannot move your head at all, scholars differ on the minimum movement required — some allow intention alone in extreme cases, while others require whatever movement is physically possible.

Do not omit an entire prayer if you can pray with reduced movements. The Prophet ﷺ taught us to use concessions step by step rather than abandoning Salah.

unable.title: Complete inability to pray
unable.body:
If you lose consciousness, fall into deep sleep through a prayer time, or are so severely ill that you cannot pray even with all position concessions — and the entire time for that prayer passes — that prayer is waived with no sin, but must be made up (Qaza) when you recover.

Marking a day as excused (illness) in this app pauses obligatory tracking and holds your streak — it does not replace the obligation to make up missed prayers later.

For chronic or long-term illness, learn the fixed concessions that apply to your situation from a qualified scholar rather than assuming every day is fully waived.

fastingQaza.title: Fasting, recovery & make-up (Qaza)
fastingQaza.body:
If fasting in Ramadan would worsen your illness or delay recovery, break the fast and make it up on other days after you recover — the Qur'an explicitly permits this for the ill.

Each missed Ramadan fast is made up with one day of fasting later; there is no kaffarah (expiation) unless the fast was broken without a valid excuse.

Missed Salah during illness must also be made up in order once you are able — unlike hayd, where missed prayers are not Qaza. When you recover, resume normal tracking and work through your Qaza at a sustainable pace.

sick.disclaimer: This is educational guidance, not a personal ruling. How much illness justifies each concession varies by school and severity — consult a qualified scholar for your situation.

events.title: Islamic events
events.subtitle: Upcoming dates in the Hijri year
events.disclaimer: Dates follow crescent visibility at your location (or the official Umm al-Qura calendar in regions that use it) and can differ by a day from a local authority announcement.

descriptions.newYear: The first of Muharram opens the Hijri (lunar) year, whose count begins from the Prophet's migration (Hijrah) from Makkah to Madinah. Muharram is one of the four sacred months and the Prophet ﷺ called it "the month of Allah," naming its voluntary fasting the best after Ramadan (Sahih Muslim 1163). It is a time to reflect on the year past and renew good intentions. There is no specific mandated ritual for the day itself, so beware of unfounded "New Year" practices; increasing voluntary fasting across the month is the established Sunnah.
descriptions.ashura: The 10th of Muharram. The Prophet ﷺ found the Jews of Madinah fasting it in gratitude for Allah saving Musa and the Children of Israel from Pharaoh, and said, "We have more right to Musa than you," then fasted it and told the Muslims to fast (Sahih al-Bukhari 2004). Fasting Ashura expiates the minor sins of the previous year (Sahih Muslim 1162). To differ from other communities, it is recommended to also fast the 9th (Tasu'a): the Prophet ﷺ intended to do so the following year (Sahih Muslim 1134). Fasting the 9th and 10th together is the preferred practice.
descriptions.mawlid: The 12th of Rabi al-Awwal is widely associated with the birth of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ (the exact date is debated among historians). Muslims universally love and honor him and are commanded to send blessings upon him (Qur'an 33:56). Whether to hold a dedicated annual celebration (Mawlid) is a point on which mainstream scholars differ: many, especially in the Sufi and traditional traditions, permit or encourage gatherings of remembrance and sending salawat, while others (notably in the Salafi tradition) hold that a fixed yearly observance was not practiced by the early generations and so should be avoided. This app presents the day neutrally; increasing salawat and following the Prophet's Sunnah are agreed goods.
descriptions.isra: Al-Isra wa al-Mi'raj commemorates the Prophet's ﷺ miraculous Night Journey from Makkah to Jerusalem (al-Aqsa) and his ascension through the heavens, referenced in Qur'an 17:1 and 53. On this night the five daily prayers were prescribed — originally fifty, then reduced to five by Allah's mercy while their reward remained fifty (Sahih al-Bukhari 349). The night affirms the sanctity of al-Aqsa and the centrality of Salah. Its precise date (commonly placed on 27 Rajab) is not firmly established, and no specific worship is authentically tied to the night itself; guarding the five daily prayers is its lasting lesson.
descriptions.ramadan: The ninth month and the fourth pillar of Islam. Fasting from dawn to sunset is obligatory on every capable adult Muslim (Qur'an 2:183–185). It is the month in which the Qur'an was first revealed (Qur'an 2:185). The Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward will have his past sins forgiven" (Sahih al-Bukhari 38). Nights are enlivened with Tarawih prayer, and the last ten days carry Laylat al-Qadr. It is a month of fasting, Qur'an, charity, and drawing near to Allah.
descriptions.laylatQadr: The Night of Decree — "better than a thousand months" (Qur'an 97:3), the night the Qur'an began to descend. Worship on it outweighs a lifetime of over eighty-three years. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever stands (in prayer) on Laylat al-Qadr out of faith and seeking reward will have his past sins forgiven" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1901). Its exact night is hidden; seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan — the 21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th, and 29th (Sahih al-Bukhari 2017), with the 27th especially hoped for. Spend these nights in prayer, Qur'an, and the dua: "Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbu al-'afwa fa'fu 'anni."
descriptions.eidFitr: The Festival of Breaking the Fast, on the 1st of Shawwal, marks the end of Ramadan. The day begins with the Eid prayer and is preceded by Zakat al-Fitr, a charity given before the prayer so the poor may also rejoice. Muslims recite the takbir, wear their best, exchange greetings, and strengthen family and community ties. Fasting is forbidden on this day (Sahih al-Bukhari 1991) — it is a day of gratitude and permitted celebration for the worship completed in Ramadan.
descriptions.arafah: The 9th of Dhul-Hijjah, the greatest day of Hajj, when pilgrims stand in worship on the plain of Arafah — "Hajj is Arafah." It falls within the blessed first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah, days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than any others (Sahih al-Bukhari 969). For those not on Hajj, fasting this day is highly recommended: it expiates the sins of the previous year and the coming year (Sahih Muslim 1162). Pilgrims themselves do not fast, so as to have strength for the standing and supplication.
descriptions.eidAdha: The Festival of Sacrifice, on the 10th of Dhul-Hijjah, is the greater of the two Eids and coincides with the culmination of Hajj. It commemorates Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to Allah, who ransomed him with a ram (Qur'an 37:100–107). Those able offer a sacrifice (Udhiyah/Qurbani), sharing the meat with family, neighbors, and the poor. The day begins with the Eid prayer and takbir and continues through the three days of Tashriq. Fasting is forbidden on this day and the days of Tashriq (Sahih al-Bukhari 1991).

basics.title: What is zakat?
basics.summary: The third pillar — 2.5% on qualifying wealth
basics.body:
Zakat is the third pillar of Islam, sitting between the prayer (Salah) and the fast of Ramadan. In the Qur'an the command to establish prayer and give zakat is repeated many times as a single pairing — showing that worship of Allah and care for His creation are woven together. It is not an optional gift but a fixed, compulsory right that the poor hold over the wealth of the rich.

The word zakat means both purification and growth. Giving a small, fixed portion of your surplus purifies the rest of your wealth and your heart from greed, and — by Allah's promise — causes what remains to grow in blessing rather than shrink.

The standard rate on monetary wealth is one-fortieth, that is 2.5%. So for every 1,000 of qualifying wealth that has completed its lunar year above the threshold, 25 is due. This is a modest share by design: enough to circulate resources to those in need without straining the giver.

Zakat is not the same as sadaqah. Sadaqah is any voluntary charity, given in any amount, at any time, to almost anyone. Zakat is a defined obligation — a set rate, on set categories of wealth, once set conditions are met, paid to set categories of people. Neglecting it deliberately is a serious sin; both the Qur'an and Sunnah warn sternly against hoarding wealth while withholding its due.

purpose.title: Why zakat — purpose & wisdom
purpose.summary: It purifies wealth and the soul, and lifts the poor
purpose.body:
Allah says of zakat: "Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow" (Qur'an 9:103). The obligation works on two levels at once — it purifies the giver's soul from stinginess and love of the world, and it purifies the wealth itself so that what stays in your hand is wholesome and blessed.

Socially, zakat is a divinely ordered system of circulation. When the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh to Yemen he instructed that zakat be taken from their rich and given to their poor. Wealth is not meant to pile up among a few; zakat pulls it back into motion so the needy are fed, debtors are freed, and the community's bonds are strengthened.

Spiritually, giving zakat is an act of gratitude and trust. It answers the human urge to hoard with the certainty that provision comes from Allah, and it trains the believer to love giving. The one who pays zakat willingly finds their wealth protected, their heart lightened, and their reward stored with their Lord — "there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve" (Qur'an 2:277).

hawl.title: The lunar year (hawl)
hawl.summary: Wealth must stay above nisab for one Hijri year
hawl.body:
Zakat on cash, gold, silver, and trade wealth is generally due only after that wealth has remained at or above the nisab threshold for one complete Hijri (lunar) year, known as the hawl. The Prophet ﷺ taught that there is no zakat on wealth until a year has passed over it.

In practice, note the date your zakatable wealth first reached nisab. That date becomes your annual zakat anniversary — each year, on that same Hijri date, you value everything you own and pay 2.5% of the total.

You do not need to track each coin separately. Most scholars hold that as long as your total stays at or above nisab across the year, small dips and rises in between do not matter — you simply assess the whole sum on your anniversary. If your wealth falls entirely below nisab during the year, many scholars consider the hawl to reset, restarting only when you next reach nisab.

Remember that the Hijri (lunar) year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year. If you prefer to pay on a fixed Gregorian date for convenience, some scholars permit it provided you slightly increase the rate to account for the shorter lunar cycle. Agricultural produce and livestock follow their own timing rules and are not tied to the hawl in the same way.

nisab.title: Nisab — the minimum threshold
nisab.summary: Measured against ~87.5 g gold or ~595–612 g silver
nisab.body:
Nisab is the minimum amount of wealth a person must own before zakat becomes obligatory. Someone whose net wealth stays below nisab all year owes no zakat — the obligation is only on those who have a genuine surplus.

The Prophet ﷺ fixed the thresholds in the currency of his time: 20 dinars of gold or 200 dirhams of silver. In weight this works out to roughly 85–87.5 g of gold, and roughly 595–612 g of silver (the small variation reflects different scholarly conversions of the dirham). This calculator uses widely cited figures of about 87.48 g gold and 612.36 g silver.

Because gold and silver no longer trade at the ratio they did in the Prophet's era, the two thresholds now give very different monetary values — the silver nisab is far lower. Many contemporary scholars therefore advise measuring cash and mixed wealth against the silver nisab: it makes more people liable, but that means more of the poor are helped, which is the spirit of the obligation. Others follow the gold nisab. Both positions are respected — follow your own scholar's guidance.

zakatable.title: What is generally zakatable
zakatable.summary: Cash, metals, investments, trade goods, receivables
zakatable.body:
Zakat is due on wealth that has the potential to grow — money and things held as money — rather than on items you simply use. The main categories agreed upon across the schools are cash, gold and silver, trade goods, and (with their own rules) crops and livestock.

Commonly zakatable today: cash in hand and in bank accounts; gold and silver, including bullion, coins, and stored jewelry not in regular use; stocks, shares, and mutual funds valued at their current market price; the merchandise and inventory of a business (trade goods), valued at resale price; strong receivables — loans and invoices you reasonably expect to collect; and rental or business income you have saved rather than spent.

Many scholars also include accessible retirement savings and cryptocurrencies held as an asset, treating them like cash or investments. When in doubt, the guiding question is simple: is this wealth a store of value or a means of growth that I could liquidate? If so, it is likely zakatable. Value everything at today's market price on your zakat date — not at what you originally paid.

exempt.title: What is usually not zakatable
exempt.summary: Personal use items, worn jewelry, locked pensions
exempt.body:
Wealth tied up in your ordinary daily life is generally not zakatable, because zakat targets growing wealth, not the things you live with and use. Your home, your car, your clothing, furniture, appliances, and the tools and equipment of your trade are all exempt — however valuable they are.

Gold and silver jewelry that a woman wears regularly is a well-known point of difference. The Hanafi school holds that all gold and silver is zakatable even if worn; the majority — Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali — exempt jewelry kept for normal personal use but include it if it is hoarded as a store of wealth or exceeds customary adornment. Follow the ruling of the school you follow.

Pension or provident funds you cannot yet access are often excluded until the money actually comes into your hands, though some scholars require zakat on the accessible portion. Debts owed to you that are unlikely ever to be repaid are usually not counted until recovered. As always, the finer details vary between schools — when a case is unclear, ask a qualified scholar rather than guess.

debts.title: Debts & deductions
debts.summary: Immediate debts may be deducted before calculating 2.5%
debts.body:
Zakat is calculated on your net zakatable wealth, so genuine debts you owe can reduce the amount on which you pay. The clearest case is debts due now — an unpaid personal loan, an outstanding credit-card balance, rent or bills already owed. Most scholars allow these to be subtracted from your gross wealth before you apply the 2.5%.

Long-term debts such as a mortgage or a multi-year installment plan are handled with more care, because deducting the entire balance would wipe out the zakat of almost anyone with a home loan. A common contemporary approach is to deduct only the payments due within the coming year, not the whole outstanding sum. Schools and scholars differ here, so pick a consistent method under guidance.

Two cautions. First, do not treat future or hypothetical expenses as deductible debts — only what you actually owe counts. Second, do not subtract last year's unpaid zakat as if it were an ordinary debt; unpaid zakat remains a due obligation and should simply be paid. When your debt situation is complex, a scholar's ruling is worth more than a rough guess.

recipients.title: Who may receive zakat
recipients.body:
Zakat may only be given to the categories of people Allah Himself named in Surah at-Tawbah (9:60). This is one of the few acts of worship where the recipients are fixed by revelation, not left to the giver's preference. The eight categories are: the poor (al-fuqara); the needy (al-masakin); those employed to collect and administer zakat; those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-mu'allafah); the freeing of captives and those in bondage (fi'r-riqab); the debt-burdened (al-gharimin); in the cause of Allah (fi sabil Allah); and the stranded traveler (ibn as-sabil).

It is not required to give to all eight; giving your zakat to even one eligible category fulfills the obligation, and directing it to the poor and needy is the most common practice.

Equally important is who may not receive it. Zakat cannot be given to the wealthy, nor to those you are already obliged to support — your parents, your children, or your spouse — since supporting them is a duty you owe anyway. In the classical view it is a personal transfer of ownership to an eligible individual, not a general donation; scholars differ on whether institutions such as masjids or broad public projects qualify under the cause of Allah. It also cannot be given to the family of the Prophet ﷺ, the Banu Hashim, as zakat. Aim it deliberately at people who match the Qur'anic categories.

otherRates.title: Other types of zakat & zakat al-fitr
otherRates.summary: Crops, livestock, and the pre-Eid zakat al-fitr differ
otherRates.body:
The 2.5% rate applies to money and trade wealth — zakat al-mal, which this calculator covers. Several other categories have entirely different rules and rates.

Crops and fruit have zakat due at harvest, not after a year: the rate is 10% (ushr) for land watered naturally by rain or springs, and 5% for land irrigated by artificial effort or cost. Grazing livestock — camels, cattle, sheep, and goats that graze freely for most of the year — have their own species-by-species nisab counts and sliding scales, drawn directly from the Sunnah.

Zakat al-fitr is different again, and every Muslim should know it. It is a small, fixed charity — about one sa' (roughly 2.5–3 kg) of a staple food such as dates, barley, wheat, or rice, or its cash value in many rulings — due at the end of Ramadan on behalf of every member of the household, young and old. Its purpose is to purify the fasting person from any shortfall and to ensure the poor also have food to celebrate Eid. The Prophet ﷺ commanded that it be paid before the Eid al-Fitr prayer; paid afterwards it counts only as ordinary charity. Each of these categories has its own detailed rulings — seek guidance specific to the asset.

mistakes.title: Common mistakes to avoid
mistakes.summary: Errors that make zakat invalid or miscalculated
mistakes.body:
Even sincere Muslims often slip on the practical details of zakat. Knowing the common errors helps you pay correctly and with peace of mind.

Forgetting the hawl or the anniversary: paying at a random time, or skipping years, leaves an outstanding obligation. Fix one Hijri date each year and assess your wealth on it.

Miscounting wealth: valuing gold or shares at their purchase price instead of today's market value, forgetting cash held in multiple accounts or currencies, or overlooking business inventory and money owed to you. Zakat is on everything zakatable that you own on your date.

Giving to the wrong people: handing zakat to parents, children, or a spouse you already support, or treating it as a generic donation to any good cause. It must reach one of the eight Qur'anic categories.

Intention errors: giving generously all year but never intending any of it as zakat. Zakat is an act of worship and needs the intention (niyyah) that this particular payment is your obligatory zakat.

Over-deducting debts: subtracting a whole long-term mortgage, or future expenses that are not yet owed, to shrink the bill. Only real, current liabilities reduce your zakatable wealth. When any of these is unclear for your situation, ask a qualified scholar rather than assume.

quran.excerpt: Zakat expenditures are only for the poor and for the needy and for those employed to collect it and for bringing hearts together and for freeing captives and for those in debt and for the cause of Allah and for the wayfarer — an obligation from Allah. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.

hadith.excerpt: Islam is built upon five: the testimony that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, paying zakat, pilgrimage to the House, and fasting Ramadan.
The Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh to Yemen and said: Teach them that Allah has made charity (zakat) obligatory upon them — taken from their rich and returned to their poor.

There is no owner of gold or silver who does not pay what is due on it except that on the Day of Resurrection plates of fire will be made for him, heated in the Fire of Hell, and his side, forehead, and back will be seared with them.

currency.title: Currency & rates
currency.body: Zakat is calculated on the market value of your wealth in a currency you understand. Spot gold and silver prices help estimate nisab and metal values — they are indicative, not a substitute for local market rates used by your scholar.

liquid.title: Cash & precious metals
liquid.body: Cash, bank balances, and gold or silver held as wealth are among the clearest zakatable assets. The Prophet ﷺ warned sternly about withholding what is due on gold and silver. Jewelry worn for normal use is a known point of difference between schools — follow your madhhab. You may enter a cash value here, or calculate metals by weight in the next section.

metals.title: Gold & silver by weight
metals.body: Nisab was fixed in the Sunnah by weight: about 20 dinars of gold or 200 dirhams of silver (commonly cited as ~87.5 g gold or ~612 g silver). Karat and purity matter because zakat is on the pure metal content. Live prices are for 24k / fine metal per gram — choose your unit (gram, tola, troy oz) and karat so the calculator converts correctly.

investments.title: Investments & business
investments.body: Trade goods, merchandise, and wealth meant to grow are generally zakatable at today's market value. Shares and funds are commonly valued like trade wealth. Strong receivables you expect to collect are often included. Qur'an 2:267 urges spending from the good of what you have earned — value honestly on your zakat date.

property.title: Land, property & vehicles
property.body: Your personal home, personal car, and ordinary household goods are generally not zakatable — zakat targets growing wealth, not items of use. Plots, houses, or vehicles held for investment, sale, or trade may be included at market value (or amounts already paid on installment investment plots). When unsure, ask a scholar.

livestock.title: Livestock (grazing flocks)
livestock.body: Free-grazing sheep, goats, cattle, and camels have their own Sunnah scales and animal nisab (e.g. 40 sheep, 30 cattle, 5 camels) — not the 2.5% money rate. Due is usually paid in animals of specified age. Fed animals kept as a business often follow trade-goods rules instead. Optional cash values here are only a planning estimate.

agriculture.title: Agriculture & harvest (ushr)
agriculture.body: Zakat on crops is due at harvest, not after a lunar year. The well-known rate is 10% (ushr) when land is watered by rain or springs, and 5% when irrigation costs effort or money. Enter this season's harvest market value and choose the water source that matches your situation.
agriculture.localRefExcerpt: And He is the One Who produces gardens, trellised and untrellised, and palm trees and crops of different [flavours], and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest…

deductions.title: Deductions
deductions.body: Zakat is on net zakatable wealth. Immediate debts due now are commonly deducted before applying 2.5%. Long-term mortgages are treated more carefully — many contemporary scholars deduct only the coming year's payments, not the whole balance. Living expenses due immediately are allowed only if your scholar permits.

nisab.title: Nisab threshold
nisab.body: Nisab is the minimum surplus before wealth zakat is due. The Prophet ﷺ fixed it at 20 dinars of gold or 200 dirhams of silver, and taught that no zakat is due until a year has passed over the wealth. Because gold and silver prices diverge today, many scholars prefer the lower (often silver) threshold so more of the poor are helped. This calculator suggests the lower of the two live estimates.

paths.body: Each deed includes evidence, practical steps, and links to Munib trackers.

journey.title: My journey
journey.body: See today's consistency in Salah, adhkar, and reflection — not a rank score.

tasbeehStyles.title: Choose your tasbeeh style
tasbeehStyles.body: Count on a ring, sliding beads, a digital clicker or a dark focus screen, with optional click sounds. Tap Style on any counter.

voluntaryFasting.title: Voluntary fasting
voluntaryFasting.body: Plan Mondays and Thursdays, Arafah, Ashura and the six of Shawwal, get a gentle reminder the night before, and see the days on which fasting is not allowed.

quranNotes.title: Your notes on the Qur'an
quranNotes.body: Write your own reflections on any ayah, highlight it in a color, add tags, and find everything again in My Qur'an notes.

selfReview.title: Private reflection & family ties
selfReview.body: A one-minute nightly muhasabah and gentle reminders to keep in touch with family — encrypted, visible only to you.

rawatib.title: Track the Sunnah rawatib
rawatib.body: Tap the small chips under each Salah on the tracker to log the Sunnah before and after it — 12 or 10 rakahs a day, following your madhhab.

debtsWasiyyah.title: Debts, trusts & your wasiyyah
debtsWasiyyah.body: Keep a private record of what you owe and hold in trust, then write a guided Islamic will that pays debts first.

dhulHijjah.title: The best ten days
dhulHijjah.body: In Dhul-Hijjah, follow the ten days, the Day of Arafah, Takbir al-Tashriq for your madhhab and your udhiyah plan.

sunnahHabits.title: Keep a few daily sunnahs
sunnahHabits.body: Pick a small list of everyday sunnahs, each with its reference. Gentle dots show how often you kept them.

quranRoots.title: Search by Arabic root
quranRoots.body: Type or pick the root letters to see every word from that root in the Qur'an, grouped by lemma, and jump to each ayah.

mirath.title: Inheritance calculator
mirath.body: Work out the shares of the heirs under any of the four schools, with each share explained and the schools compared.

umrahMode.title: Umrah, step by step
umrahMode.body: During Umrah, follow each rite in order with tawaf and sa'i counters, a miqat alert and duas from Hisnul Muslim.

focusLock.title: Salah focus lock
focusLock.body: Pause distracting apps around each Salah until you pray. Calls and messages are never blocked.

coach.title: Weekly gentle coach
coach.body: Once a week, a few kind, actionable steps from your own tracking — worked out on your device, never sent anywhere.

partnerKhatm.title: Partner & group khatm
partnerKhatm.body: Encourage a friend with a quiet "done" and a dua for each other, or finish the Qur'an together by sharing out its parts.

familyKids.title: Family & kids mode
familyKids.body: Help your children grow into Salah gently. Parents see only the five fard statuses and their child's stickers — no comparisons, no notes.

masjids.title: Masjids near you
masjids.body: Find nearby masjids from OpenStreetMap, set your home masjid, and keep your own iqamah times, typed in or read from a photo of the timetable.

quranPractice.title: Recite with the Qur'an listener
quranPractice.body: Follow, check or revise any passage — the words light up as you recite, on your device.

reciteToFind.title: Recite to find an ayah
reciteToFind.body: Recite a few words and the app finds the ayah. Audio stays on your device.

handsFreeSequence.title: Hands-free after-Salah tasbeeh
handsFreeSequence.body: 33 · 33 · 34 that counts as you say each Zikr and moves on by itself. Tap to correct any miscount.

sahaba.title: Sahaba
sahaba.subtitle: Short profiles of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ
sahaba.intro: The sahaba are the generation that carried Islam from the Prophet ﷺ to the rest of the world. These short profiles follow the tone of the seerah timeline — a life, a lesson, and a source for every claim.

categoryHint.family: Close family of the Prophet ﷺ
categoryHint.women: Prominent women of the early community

sahaba.exploreBattlesHint: Companions who appear in the military campaigns
sahaba.exploreSeerahHint: Life of the Prophet ﷺ through key milestones
sahaba.exploreHistoryHint: From the Prophet's ﷺ passing to the end of the Rashidun
sahaba.noResults: No companions in this category yet
sahaba.readMore: Tap to read the full profile
sahaba.disclaimer: Narrative facts follow the classical seerah and history works; every claim tied to a specific narration cites its hadith collection and number. This is general educational content, not a scholarly ranking.

history.title: Early Islamic history
history.subtitle: From the Prophet's ﷺ death to the end of the Rashidun Caliphate
history.disclaimer: Scoped to 11–41 AH (632–661 CE) — the close of the Prophet's ﷺ life through the end of the Rashidun Caliphate. Political and military narrative follows the classical history works; the Uthman/Ali period is presented without adjudicating later theological disputes.

laylatAlQadr.title: Laylat al-Qadr
laylatAlQadr.subtitle: The Night of Decree — better than a thousand months
laylatAlQadr.intro: Laylat al-Qadr is hidden among the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan, not fixed to a single date. Seek it with sincere worship across all of them rather than one guessed night.
laylatAlQadr.disclaimer: This guide does not endorse a single fixed calendar date or folk 'signs' for identifying the night — only what the Qur'an and authentic hadith state.

eid.title: Eid guide
eid.subtitle: Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha — prayer, Sunnah, and rulings
eid.intro: The two Eids from the Qur'an and authentic hadith — how to pray Eid Salah, Zakat al-Fitr, udhiyah, and the Sunnah practices of the day.
eid.disclaimer: Educational overview — not a fatwa. Where schools differ (such as the extra-takbir count), both positions are presented; follow your imam or a qualified local scholar.

friday.title: Friday & Jumu'ah
friday.subtitle: Virtues, preparation, Surah al-Kahf, salawat, and the hour of dua
friday.intro: Friday is the best day the sun rises on. Learn the authentic practices of Jumu'ah — ghusl, the prayer, Surah al-Kahf, salawat, and seeking the accepted hour — from the Qur'an and sahih hadith.
friday.disclaimer: Educational overview — not a fatwa. Where schools differ (such as whether Friday ghusl is wajib or Sunnah mu'akkadah), both positions are noted; follow your imam or a qualified local scholar.

whiteDays.title: White Days fasting
whiteDays.subtitle: Ayyām al-Bīḍ — the Sunnah fast of the 13th, 14th and 15th
whiteDays.intro: Fasting three days each month is a beloved Sunnah, and the White Days — the 13th, 14th and 15th of each Hijri month — are the chosen three. Learn their virtue, how to observe them, and the evidence from the Qur'an and sahih hadith.
whiteDays.disclaimer: Educational overview — not a fatwa. The exact dates depend on the Hijri month, which varies by moon sighting; follow your local masjid or a qualified scholar for religious dates and rulings.

ruqyah.title: Ruqyah
ruqyah.subtitle: Qur'anic and prophetic spiritual healing
ruqyah.intro: Ruqyah is reciting Qur'an, Allah's Names, or authentic prophetic supplications for healing and protection — never a substitute for Salah or medical care.
ruqyah.disclaimer: Ruqyah is a spiritual practice, not a medical treatment. It does not replace seeing a qualified doctor, nor the five daily prayers. For serious or persistent affliction, consult both a scholar and a medical professional.

newMuslim.title: New Muslim guide
newMuslim.subtitle: A warm, practical start for the first days and weeks
newMuslim.intro: Welcome to Islam. This guide covers the shahada, the five pillars, the basics of faith, and a first look at prayer, then points you to the fuller Salah, Aqeedah, and Qur'an guides in this app.
newMuslim.disclaimer: A shallow-but-correct starting guide covering only the shared essentials every school agrees on. For your specific situation, ask a local imam or teacher.

finance.title: Islamic finance
finance.subtitle: Riba, fair trade, giving, and takaful
finance.intro: An educational introduction to the ethical framework Islam brings to money — the prohibition of riba, fair trade, zakah and sadaqah, and takaful (cooperative risk-sharing).
finance.disclaimer: General education, not financial or fatwa advice. Fund screeners, specific products, and rulings on your own contracts need a qualified, certified Islamic finance scholar or institution.

dateConverter.title: Date converter
dateConverter.subtitle: Convert between the Hijri and Gregorian calendars
dateConverter.intro: Enter a date in either calendar to see its equivalent in the other, calculated offline from crescent visibility at your location.
dateConverter.quickCalendarHint: Browse months with your prayer log
dateConverter.quickEventsHint: Upcoming dates on the Hijri calendar

dateConverter.disclaimer: Dates are calculated from crescent (hilāl) visibility at your location and can differ by a day from official moon-sighting announcements — always follow your local masjid or authority for religious dates.

fidyah.title: Fidyah & kaffarah
fidyah.subtitle: Estimate helpers for missed or broken Ramadan fasts — not auto-rulings
fidyah.intro: Use this only as a planning estimate. Qur'an 2:184–185 and Sahih Muslim 1111 frame the basics; a qualified scholar must classify whether you owe Qaza, fidyah, kaffarah, or something else.
fidyah.helperHint: Enter days and your local meal or fidya unit cost. Prefer a rate published by a trusted local masjid or council.

janazah.title: Janazah guide
janazah.subtitle: Funeral prayer, washing, burial, and authentic duas
janazah.intro: A practical overview of Janazah as a communal obligation — four takbirs without ruku or sujud, Hisnul Muslim duas for men, women, and children, and guidance for washing, burial, martyrs, and the bereaved.
janazah.disclaimer: Educational overview — not a funeral director's manual or a fatwa. Confirm washing, shrouding, and cemetery practice with qualified local guidance.

pebbles.desc: Each count moves one date pit or pebble from one dish to the other. The note explains the evidence and how scholars grade it.

pebbles.body: A report tells of a woman who counted her tasbeeh on date pits or pebbles in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ; he taught her a fuller wording and is not reported to have objected. Scholars grade this report differently. Many allow counting with pebbles, date pits or beads, while others hold that counting on the fingertips is better. Every design counts exactly the same.
pebbles.tirmidhi3568: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3568 — hasan gharib (at-Tirmidhi), hasan (Bashar Awwad Ma'ruf), da'if (al-Albani), munkar (Ahmad Shakir)
pebbles.abudawud1500: Sunan Abu Dawud 1500 — hasan li-ghayrihi (Shu'aib al-Arna'ut), da'if (al-Albani)

fingers.body: The Prophet ﷺ taught counting Zikr on the fingertips. This hand is only a visual aid — your own finger method is fine, whichever way you were taught to count. Every design counts exactly the same.
fingers.abudawud1501: Sunan Abu Dawud 1501 — counting on the fingertips: hasan (al-Albani, Shu'aib al-Arna'ut)
fingers.tirmidhi3583: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3583 — gradings differ: hasan (Ahmad Shakir), da'if (al-Albani)

start.title: When Asr begins
start.hanafi: When an object's shadow is twice its length (plus its shadow at midday).
start.majority: When an object's shadow equals its length (plus its shadow at midday).

preferred.title: Preferred time for Asr
preferred.hanafi: Delaying it is preferred, as long as the sun has not turned yellow.
preferred.majority: Praying it early in its time is preferred.

preferred.title: Preferred time for Fajr
preferred.hanafi: Isfar: once the dawn light has spread, leaving time to repeat the Salah if needed.
preferred.majority: Taghlis: early, while it is still dark.

start.title: When Isha begins (for information)
start.hanafi: After the white twilight disappears (Abu Hanifa). Many Hanafi fatwas follow his two students: after the red twilight.

preferred.title: Preferred time for Isha
preferred.delay: Delaying it to a third of the night is preferred.
preferred.shafii: Praying it early is preferred (another view in the school prefers delaying it).
preferred.maliki: Praying it early is preferred, especially for congregations.
preferred.hanbali: Delaying it to a third of the night is preferred, if that is not hard on others.

form.title: How Witr is prayed
form.hanafi: Three rakahs with one salam; qunut before ruku in the third rakah, all year.
form.shafii: At least one rakah, commonly three (two, then one), at most eleven; qunut after ruku in the second half of Ramadan.
form.maliki: One rakah prayed after a separate two-rakah shaf'; no qunut in Witr.
form.hanbali: At least one rakah, commonly three, at most eleven; qunut after ruku, all year.

qaza.title: Making up a missed Witr
qaza.hanafi: Required: a missed Witr is made up as Qaza.
qaza.recommended: Recommended: it is good to make it up.
qaza.maliki: Not made up once the Fajr Salah has been prayed.

raisingHands.title: Raising the hands in Salah
raisingHands.shafii: With the opening takbir, before ruku, on rising from ruku, and on standing for the third rakah.
raisingHands.maliki: Only with the opening takbir (the school's well-known view).
raisingHands.hanbali: With the opening takbir, before ruku, and on rising from ruku.

fatihaBehindImam.title: Reciting Al-Fatihah behind the imam
fatihaBehindImam.hanafi: Not recited: the follower listens, and the imam's recitation suffices.
fatihaBehindImam.shafii: Obligatory for the follower in every rakah of every Salah.
fatihaBehindImam.maliki: Recited in the silent salahs; in the loud ones the follower listens.
fatihaBehindImam.hanbali: Recommended in the silent salahs and in the imam's pauses; otherwise the follower listens.

fajrQunut.title: Qunut in Fajr
fajrQunut.shafii: Sunnah: said standing after ruku in the second rakah.
fajrQunut.maliki: Recommended: said quietly before ruku in the second rakah.
fajrQunut.hanbali: Not done, except qunut at times of calamity (nazilah).

lastSitting.title: How to sit in the final tashahhud
lastSitting.hanafi: Iftirash (sitting on the left foot, right foot upright) in every sitting, including the last.
lastSitting.shafii: Tawarruk (sitting on the ground, left foot under the right leg) in the final sitting of every Salah, including two-rakah salahs; iftirash in the others.
lastSitting.maliki: Tawarruk in every sitting, the first and the last.
lastSitting.hanbali: Tawarruk only in the final sitting of a Salah with two tashahhuds (three or four rakahs); iftirash otherwise.

firstTashahhud.title: Ruling of the first tashahhud
firstTashahhud.wajib: Wajib: if forgotten, sujud as-sahw repairs the Salah.
firstTashahhud.sunnah: Sunnah: if forgotten, it is made up for with sujud as-sahw.

abandoning.title: Ruling on one who abandons Salah
abandoning.majority: A grave major sin; the person remains a Muslim as long as they do not deny that Salah is obligatory.
abandoning.hanbali: The relied-upon view: whoever persists in abandoning it after being called to it by the authorities is judged to have left Islam.

sunnah.title: Sunnah Salah before and after Jumu'ah
sunnah.hanafi: Four rakahs before and four after, both Sunnah mu'akkadah (Abu Yusuf: six after — many pray four, then two).
sunnah.shafii: Like Dhuhr: two rakahs before and two after are emphasized; four and four complete it.
sunnah.maliki: No fixed (ratibah) Sunnah before or after; voluntary Salah is allowed.
sunnah.hanbali: No fixed Sunnah before (voluntary Salah before it is recommended); after it, at least two rakahs and up to six.

status.title: Ruling of the Eid Salah
status.hanafi: Wajib for those who must attend Jumu'ah.

extraTakbirs.title: Extra takbirs in the Eid Salah
extraTakbirs.hanafi: Three in each rakah: before the recitation in the first, after it in the second.
extraTakbirs.shafii: Seven in the first rakah and five in the second, besides the opening takbir and the takbir of standing.
extraTakbirs.sixFive: Six in the first rakah (seven counting the opening takbir) and five in the second.

fatiha.title: Al-Fatihah in the janazah Salah
fatiha.hanafi: Not recited as recitation; praise of Allah follows the first takbir.
fatiha.maliki: Not recited; the takbirs are followed by praise and dua.

preset.title: Default Sunnah rawatib in the app
preset.hanafi: 12 rakahs: 2 before Fajr, 4 before and 2 after Dhuhr, 2 after Maghrib, 2 after Isha.
preset.ten: 10 rakahs: 2 before Fajr, 2 before and 2 after Dhuhr, 2 after Maghrib, 2 after Isha.
preset.maliki: The app uses the 10-rakah preset. Maliki texts encourage voluntary Salah around these times without fixing a number.

fajrMakeup.title: Making up the Fajr Sunnah
fajrMakeup.hanafi: Made up together with a missed Fajr, before midday. If only the Sunnah was missed it is not made up (Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf); Muhammad allowed it after sunrise until midday.
fajrMakeup.recommended: Recommended to make it up if missed, including after sunrise.
fajrMakeup.maliki: The one nafl that is made up — after sunrise, until midday (zawal).

rakahs.title: Number of Tarawih rakahs (for information)
rakahs.maliki: Twenty; thirty-six was the older practice of the people of Madinah.

takbir.title: Takbir al-Tashriq after the obligatory salahs
takbir.hanafi: Wajib, from Fajr on the 9th to Asr on the 13th of Dhul-Hijjah; it begins with two takbirs.
takbir.shafii: Sunnah, from Fajr on the 9th to Asr on the 13th of Dhul-Hijjah; it begins with three takbirs.
takbir.maliki: Sunnah, from Dhuhr on the 10th to Fajr on the 13th of Dhul-Hijjah; three takbirs.
takbir.hanbali: Sunnah, from Fajr on the 9th to Asr on the 13th of Dhul-Hijjah; it begins with two takbirs.

min.title: Shortest period of hayd
min.maliki: No minimum for the purposes of worship: any flow counts.

max.title: Longest period of hayd
max.maliki: Fifteen days. A woman with a regular habit adds up to three days to it (istizhar), never past fifteen.

beyondMax.title: Bleeding beyond the maximum
beyondMax.hanafi: Istihada: resume Salah, with a fresh wudu for each Salah time.
beyondMax.habitColour: Istihada: the days are sorted by her habit or by the color of the blood.
beyondMax.maliki: Istihada: resume Salah (a fresh wudu for each Salah is recommended).

quranRecitation.title: Reciting the Qur'an during hayd
quranRecitation.majority: Not recited as Qur'an. Listening is fine, and Qur'anic phrases may be said as Zikr or dua.
quranRecitation.maliki: She may recite from memory; she does not touch the mushaf.

max.title: Longest period of nifas (bleeding after childbirth)

distance.title: Distance for shortening Salah (qasr)
distance.hanafi: About 77–78 km (48 miles): three days' travel by the classical measure.
distance.majority: About 81–89 km (four burud); conversions of the old measure differ.

status.title: Ruling of shortening (qasr) on a journey
status.hanafi: Wajib: the traveler prays two rakahs, not four.

residency.title: When a traveler becomes resident
residency.hanafi: On intending to stay 15 days or more.
residency.shafii: On intending to stay 4 full days or more, not counting the days of arrival and departure.
residency.maliki: On intending to stay 4 full days (about 20 salahs) or more.
residency.hanbali: On intending to stay more than 4 days (more than 20 salahs).

travel.title: Combining salahs (jam') while traveling
travel.hanafi: Not allowed, except at Arafah and Muzdalifah during Hajj.
travel.maliki: Allowed with conditions, mainly while on the move.

rain.title: Combining salahs because of rain
rain.shafii: Allowed for Dhuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha, brought forward, in congregation.

rawatib.title: Sunnah rawatib while traveling
rawatib.hanafi: Optional while on the move, except the Fajr Sunnah; recommended once settled.
rawatib.optional: They remain Sunnah; the traveler may leave them.
rawatib.hanbali: The traveler may leave them, except the Fajr Sunnah and Witr.

nisabBasis.title: Nisab for cash and trade goods
nisabBasis.hanafi: Whichever of gold or silver is lower in value, as it is better for the poor.
nisabBasis.contested: Gold or silver. For modern currency, contemporary scholars differ; the app starts with gold and lets you change it.
nisabBasis.hanbali: The value most beneficial to the poor: in practice, the lower of gold or silver.

combineGoldSilver.title: Adding gold and silver together to reach nisab
combineGoldSilver.shafii: No: each metal is counted on its own.
combineGoldSilver.parts: Yes, by the share each makes of its own nisab.

jewellery.title: Zakat on women's personal jewelry
jewellery.hanafi: Zakat is due on gold and silver jewelry.
jewellery.majority: No zakat on permissible jewelry in normal use.

forgetfulEating.title: Eating or drinking forgetfully while fasting
forgetfulEating.majority: The fast remains valid; carry on fasting.
forgetfulEating.maliki: The fast is broken and is made up (in an obligatory fast); no kaffarah.

kaffarah.title: What requires kaffarah in Ramadan
kaffarah.eatingToo: Deliberate intercourse, or deliberately eating or drinking.

afterMidShaban.title: Voluntary fasting after mid-Sha'ban
afterMidShaban.shafii: Not permitted (the relied-upon view), unless it is a habit, joined to fasts before the 15th, Qaza or a vow.
afterMidShaban.noRule: No special restriction; fasting a day or two just before Ramadan is discouraged unless it is a habit.

measure.title: Fidyah for each missed fast
measure.hanafi: Half a sa' of wheat, or one sa' of dates or barley; giving its value in cash is allowed.
measure.shafii: One mudd of the local staple food, given as food.
measure.maliki: One mudd of the local staple food, given as food (for the very elderly it is recommended rather than required).
measure.hanbali: One mudd of wheat or half a sa' of other food, given as food.

measure.title: Sadaqat al-fitr per person
measure.hanafi: Half a sa' of wheat or one sa' of other foods; giving its value in cash is allowed.
measure.majority: One sa' of the local staple food, given as food.

wudu.title: Wudu for tawaf
wudu.hanafi: Wajib: tawaf without wudu counts but requires a penalty.
wudu.majority: A condition: tawaf without wudu does not count.

status.title: Ruling of the udhiyah (Eid sacrifice)
status.hanafi: Wajib on a resident who owns nisab; it may be slaughtered until sunset on the 12th.
status.shafii: Sunnah mu'akkadah; it may be slaughtered until sunset on the 13th.
status.sunnah12: Sunnah mu'akkadah; it may be slaughtered until sunset on the 12th.

hairNails.title: Cutting hair and nails in the first ten days (when sacrificing)
hairNails.hanbali: Not permitted (haram) until the animal is slaughtered.

grandfatherSiblings.title: The grandfather with brothers and sisters (inheritance)
grandfatherSiblings.hanafi: The grandfather excludes full and paternal siblings, like the father (Abu Hanifa's view).
grandfatherSiblings.majority: They share with him (muqasamah); he takes whichever is best for him: sharing, a third of the remainder, or a sixth.

mushtarakah.title: The shared case (al-Mushtarakah)
mushtarakah.excluded: The full brothers receive nothing once the fixed shares use up the estate.
mushtarakah.share: The full brothers share the maternal siblings' third equally with them.

paternalGrandmother.title: The paternal grandmother when the father is alive
paternalGrandmother.excluded: She is excluded by the father.
paternalGrandmother.hanbali: She still inherits: her son does not exclude her.

radd.title: Returning a surplus to the heirs (radd)
radd.heirs: The surplus returns to the fixed-share heirs, except the spouses.
radd.treasury: Classically it goes to the public treasury; later scholars return it to the heirs where there is no organized treasury.

malikiyyah.title: Grandfather, maternal siblings and a paternal brother (al-Malikiyyah)
malikiyyah.hanafi: The grandfather excludes all the siblings anyway, so he takes the remaining third.
malikiyyah.zayd: Zayd's general method applies: the grandfather and the paternal brother each take a sixth.
malikiyyah.maliki: The grandfather takes the whole remaining third; the paternal siblings get nothing (al-Malikiyyah).

intention.title: Intention (niyyah) in wudu
intention.hanafi: Sunnah: wudu without intention still lifts minor impurity, but the reward needs intention.
intention.majority: Required: wudu without intention is not valid.

tartib.title: Order (tartib) of the washes
tartib.sunnah: Sunnah: wudu done out of the Qur'anic order is still valid.
tartib.fard: Obligatory: the limbs must be washed in the Qur'anic order.

muwalat.title: Continuity (muwalat) in wudu
muwalat.sunnah: Sunnah: a pause between the washes does not invalidate wudu.
muwalat.maliki: Obligatory when remembered and able: a long deliberate break invalidates it; a forgetful one is excused.
muwalat.hanbali: Obligatory: a limb must not be left to dry before the next is washed, in normal conditions.

dalk.title: Rubbing the limbs (dalk)
dalk.majority: Sunnah: water flowing over the limb is enough; rubbing is recommended.
dalk.maliki: Obligatory: pass the hand over each washed limb with the water.

touchOppositeSex.title: Touching the opposite sex
touchOppositeSex.shafii: Breaks wudu: skin-to-skin contact between an adult man and woman who are not mahram, even without desire.
touchOppositeSex.desire: Breaks wudu only when there is desire, intended or felt.

touchPrivateParts.title: Touching the private parts
touchPrivateParts.shafii: Breaks wudu when the front or back private part is touched directly with the palm or inner fingers.
touchPrivateParts.maliki: Breaks a man's wudu when he touches his private part directly with the palm or inner fingers; for a woman, the school's scholars differ.
touchPrivateParts.hanbali: Breaks wudu when the private part is touched directly with the hand.

debtsToAllah.title: Zakat, fidyah and kaffarah still owed at death
debtsToAllah.third: Paid only if the person bequeathed them, and then from the one-third.
debtsToAllah.capital: Paid from the whole estate before bequests and inheritance, like debts to people, whether bequeathed or not.

noHeirs.title: Bequeathing more than one-third when there are no heirs at all
noHeirs.whole: Allowed: with no heir at all, the bequest may cover the whole estate.
noHeirs.third: Still limited to one-third; the rest goes to the public treasury.

tahiyyat.title: Tahiyyat al-masjid in the disliked times and during the khutbah
tahiyyat.notDislikedTimes: Sunnah, but not prayed in the times when voluntary Salah is disliked (after Fajr and Asr, at sunrise, zenith and sunset), nor once the imam has begun the Friday khutbah.
tahiyyat.shafii: Sunnah, and prayed even in the disliked times because it has a cause (entering the masjid). During the Friday khutbah, two short rakahs are prayed.
tahiyyat.hanbali: Sunnah. The relied-on view is not to pray it in the disliked times (another report from Imam Ahmad allows it); during the Friday khutbah, two short rakahs are prayed.

taqsir.title: How much a man shortens (taqsir)
taqsir.hanafi: At least a quarter of the head must be shaved or shortened.
taqsir.shafii: At least three hairs of the head, shaved or shortened, are enough.
taqsir.wholeHead: The whole head: shortening only part of it is not enough.

reason.eid: Fasting on the day of Eid is not allowed.
reason.tashriq: The days of Tashriq (11–13 Dhul-Hijjah) are days of eating, drinking and remembering Allah. Fasting them is not allowed.
reason.ramadan: This is a day of Ramadan. Log it on the Ramadan screen.
reason.dayOfDoubt: The day of doubt (30 Sha'ban): scholars differ. Many dislike fasting it, especially as a precaution for Ramadan. A Qaza fast is fine.
reason.beforeRamadan: Don't fast a day or two before Ramadan, unless it is a fast you already keep regularly, such as Mondays and Thursdays.
reason.fridayAlone: Many scholars (the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools) dislike singling out Friday for a voluntary fast; others allow it. Fast Thursday or Saturday with it.
reason.pilgrimArafah: Not recommended for a pilgrim at Arafah: the Prophet ﷺ did not fast that day during his Hajj.
reason.afterMidShabanShafii: Shafi'i school: fasting after the middle of Sha'ban is not permitted (the relied-upon view), unless it is your habit, joined to days before the 15th, a Qaza fast or a vow.
reason.afterMidShabanNote: The Shafi'i school does not permit fasting after the middle of Sha'ban without a reason; the other schools have no specific rule.
reason.hayd: No fasting during hayd (menstruation); missed Ramadan days are made up later.

mirath.title: Mirath calculator
mirath.subtitle: Islamic inheritance shares for all four schools, step by step
mirath.searchKeywords: inheritance mirath faraid heirs estate shares will awl radd asabah grandfather mushtarakah akdariyyah
mirath.disclaimer: Educational calculator — confirm with a qualified scholar or a Shariah court before dividing any estate. Unusual cases are not covered.

deceased.title: Who passed away?
deceased.hint: This decides whether a husband or wives can inherit.

spouse.title: Spouse
spouse.hint: A spouse married to the deceased at the time of death.

children.title: Children
children.hint: Sons and daughters alive at the time of death.

grandchildren.title: Son's children
grandchildren.hint: Children of a son who died before the deceased. A daughter's children are not on this list.

parents.title: Parents
parents.hint: Father and mother alive at the time of death.

grandparents.title: Grandparents
grandparents.hint: Only relatives the parents don't already exclude are shown.
grandparents.note: The paternal grandfather is the father's father. The maternal grandfather is not on this list.

siblings.title: Brothers and sisters
siblings.hint: Full: same father and mother. Paternal: same father only. Maternal: same mother only.
siblings.withFatherNote: The father excludes brothers and sisters from inheriting, but two or more of them (of any kind) still reduce the mother's share from 1/3 to 1/6, so please enter them.

extended.title: Nephews, uncles and cousins
extended.hint: Male relatives through the father's side; they inherit only what remains.

confirm.title: Before the results
confirm.hint: Count only the relatives who can inherit.

confirm.muslim: Each heir is Muslim: there is no inheritance between a Muslim and a non-Muslim (Bukhari 6764).
confirm.alive: Each heir was alive at the moment of death.
confirm.notKiller: No heir unlawfully killed the deceased: the killer does not inherit (Tirmidhi 2109).
confirm.toggle: I have counted only these heirs
confirm.noHeirs: No heirs entered yet — the result will explain what happens then.

estate.title: Estate (optional)
estate.hint: Funeral costs and debts are paid first, then bequests up to one third, then the heirs share the rest.
estate.debtsHint: Everything the deceased owed to people.
estate.bequestsHint: To non-heirs. Anything over one third is capped.

result.title: Shares — {{school}}
result.dhawuAlArham: None of the listed heirs is present. The estate goes to distant kindred (dhawu al-arham) — Hanafi and Hanbali; later Shafi'i and Maliki scholars too — and how it is divided among them needs a scholar.
result.tashih: Corrected base {{base}} so every heir gets whole shares
result.radd: The surplus was returned to the heirs (radd).

unallocated.spouse_only: {{fraction}} is left after the spouse's share {{amount}}. It goes to distant kindred (dhawu al-arham) if there are any; if there are none, scholars differ on returning it to the spouse or to the public treasury. Consult a scholar.
unallocated.treasury: {{fraction}} {{amount}} goes to the public treasury (bayt al-mal) in this setting.

result.amountEachRange: {{amount}} ({{low}}–{{high}} each, so the cents add up exactly)
result.debtsExceedEstate: The funeral costs and debts ({{owed}}) are more than the estate ({{gross}}), so nothing is left for bequests or the heirs and no amounts are shown. The fractions still show how anything left after the debts are settled would be shared.

special.umariyyatayn: 'Umariyyah case: with a spouse and both parents, the mother takes a third of what remains after the spouse — the same in all four schools.
special.mushtarakah: Mushtarakah case: the schools differ on whether full brothers share the maternal siblings' third.
special.akdariyyah: Akdariyyah case: the grandfather's and the sister's shares are pooled and divided 2:1.
special.malikiyyah: al-Malikiyyah: in the Maliki school the grandfather takes the whole remaining third here.
special.shibhMalikiyyah: Shibh al-Malikiyyah: Maliki scholars differ on this case. The result shown follows Zayd's general method — consult a scholar.
special.grandfatherSiblings: Grandfather with brothers or sisters: the grandfather takes the best of sharing as a brother, a third of what remains, or a sixth (Zayd ibn Thabit's method).

why.nothing_left: Nothing remains for them after the fixed shares.
why.husband_half: The husband takes {{fraction}} because there is no child or son's child (Qur'an 4:12).
why.husband_quarter: The husband takes {{fraction}} because there is a child or son's child (Qur'an 4:12).
why.wife_quarter: The wife takes {{fraction}} — wives share it — because there is no child or son's child (Qur'an 4:12).
why.wife_eighth: The wife takes {{fraction}} — wives share it — because there is a child or son's child (Qur'an 4:12).
why.mother_third: The mother takes {{fraction}}: no child and fewer than two siblings (Qur'an 4:11).
why.mother_sixth_descendant: The mother takes {{fraction}} because there is a child or son's child (Qur'an 4:11).
why.mother_sixth_siblings: The mother takes {{fraction}} because there are two or more siblings, even ones who don't inherit (Qur'an 4:11).
why.mother_third_of_remainder: The mother takes a third of what remains after the spouse's share: {{fraction}} of the estate.
why.father_sixth: The father takes {{fraction}} because there is a son or son's son (Qur'an 4:11).
why.father_sixth_and_residue: The father takes {{fraction}} plus whatever remains, because the descendants are only female.
why.father_residue: The father takes the residue as the nearest male relative (Bukhari 6732).
why.grandfather_sixth: The grandfather stands in the father's place and takes {{fraction}} with a son or son's son.
why.grandfather_sixth_and_residue: The grandfather stands in the father's place: {{fraction}} plus whatever remains.
why.grandfather_residue: The grandfather stands in the father's place and takes the residue.
why.grandmother_sixth: A grandmother takes {{fraction}}; two grandmothers share it (Abu Dawud 2894).
why.daughter_half: One daughter with no son takes {{fraction}} (Qur'an 4:11).
why.daughters_two_thirds: Two or more daughters with no son share {{fraction}} (Qur'an 4:11).
why.sons_daughter_half: With no son or daughter, one son's daughter takes {{fraction}}.
why.sons_daughters_two_thirds: With no son or daughter, son's daughters share {{fraction}}.
why.sons_daughter_sixth: With one daughter, son's daughters take {{fraction}} to complete two thirds (Bukhari 6736).
why.sister_half: One sister with no brother takes {{fraction}} (Qur'an 4:176).
why.paternal_sister_sixth: With one full sister, paternal sisters take {{fraction}} to complete two thirds.
why.maternal_third: Maternal siblings share {{fraction}} equally, male and female alike (Qur'an 4:12).
why.residuary_self: A residuary: takes what remains after the fixed shares (Bukhari 6732).
why.residuary_with_male: Shares the residue with {{by}}, a male taking twice a female's share (Qur'an 4:11, 4:176).
why.residuary_with_daughters: With {{by}}, the sister takes what remains (Bukhari 6736).
why.awl: The fixed shares exceed the estate, so every share was reduced in proportion ('awl).
why.radd: The surplus was returned to the fixed-share heirs in proportion (radd); spouses are not included.
why.umariyyatayn: This is one of the two 'Umariyyah cases decided by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.
why.mushtarakah_share: Mushtarakah: shares the maternal siblings' third equally with {{by}} (Shafi'i, Maliki).
why.mushtarakah_excluded: Mushtarakah: the fixed shares use the whole estate, so full siblings get nothing (Hanafi, Hanbali).
why.akdariyyah: Akdariyyah: the fixed share ({{fraction}}) is pooled with {{by}} and divided 2:1.
why.malikiyyah: al-Malikiyyah (Maliki): the grandfather takes the whole remaining third.
why.muqasamah_share: The grandfather shares with the siblings as a brother — the best of his options ({{fraction}}).
why.muqasamah_third: The grandfather takes a third (of what remains after the fixed shares) — better for him than sharing ({{fraction}}).
why.muqasamah_sixth: The grandfather takes a sixth of the estate, his minimum ({{fraction}}).
why.muqasamah_siblings: Shares with the grandfather by Zayd ibn Thabit's method (muqasamah).
why.muaddah_counted: Counted against the grandfather, then {{by}} take the portion (mu'addah).
why.muaddah_reclaim: Full sisters take back up to their fixed share ({{fraction}}) from the siblings' portion (mu'addah).

umrahMode.title: Umrah mode
umrahMode.subtitle: A live, step-by-step companion for your Umrah
umrahMode.searchKeywords: umrah mode live guide tawaf counter sai counter miqat alert ihram talbiyah halq taqsir zamzam
umrahMode.tvNote: Umrah mode counts tawaf and sa'i and checks the miqat on your phone. Here is the order of the steps.

intro.title: Your Umrah, step by step
intro.body: Follow each rite in order: miqat, ihram and talbiyah, tawaf with a 7-circuit counter, two rakahs, Zamzam, sa'i with a 7-course counter, and halq or taqsir. Your place is saved, so you can close the app and pick up where you left off.
intro.offline: Works offline. Duas come from Hisnul Muslim, and rulings that differ between the schools are labeled.

umrahMode.endMessage: Your current step and counts will be cleared. Your Umrah checklist is not affected.
umrahMode.readGuide: Read this step in the guide
